title: WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN TRYING TO REPENT BEFORE YOU EVEN KNOW HOW TO BELIEVE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN TRYING TO REPENT BEFORE YOU EVEN KNOW HOW TO BELIEVE?
Does repentance come before faith, or does faith in Jesus Christ produce repentance? The answer could change everything about how you understand salvation, grace, and the God who is calling you home.
There is a man sitting alone in his car outside a church.
The service has already started.

He can hear the worship through the walls. He knows some of the songs. He even remembers singing them years ago, back when following Jesus seemed simpler, back when he hadn't made so many decisions he now wishes he could erase.
But tonight, he cannot bring himself to open the door.
Because he has a question.
Not the kind of question people usually ask during Bible study.
The kind that keeps you awake at two in the morning.
“Do I have to change my life before I can come back to Jesus… or do I come to Jesus because I cannot change my life?”
He wants to repent.
He really does.
But he has promised God he would change before.
He has cried after committing the same sin. Deleted the same contacts. Made the same commitments. Prayed the same desperate prayers.
And somehow, he keeps ending up here.
Ashamed.
Exhausted.
Wondering whether his repentance was ever real.
Perhaps that man is closer to your story than you would like to admit.
Perhaps you have never sat outside a church, but you have sat at the edge of your bed, staring at the floor, wondering why you still struggle with something you thought you surrendered years ago.
And somewhere along the way, you began believing that Jesus would receive you once you became sufficiently repentant.
But what if the very way you have been thinking about repentance has been keeping you from understanding the grace that makes repentance possible?
What if you have been trying to produce, through your own strength, something Scripture describes as a gift God grants?
And what if the answer is not as simple as choosing whether repentance or faith comes first?
Because three passages of Scripture bring us face-to-face with a truth that is both deeply humbling and extraordinarily hopeful.
And we need to hear all three.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus begins His public proclamation with words that confront every human heart:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
In the original Greek, the command reads:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Two commands.
One Savior.
One urgent response to the arrival of God's kingdom.
The word μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) comes from μετανοέω (metanoeō), meaning to repent, to change one's mind or understanding in a way that involves a genuine turning of one's life.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling bad about what happened.
It is not simply being embarrassed because somebody discovered your sin.
It is not promising to behave better so that God will finally approve of you.
Repentance involves a real turning away from sin and toward God.
And the word πιστεύετε (pisteuete) comes from πιστεύω (pisteuō), meaning to believe, trust, or place faith in.
In the context of the Gospel, believing is more than agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is trusting the good news God has revealed in His Son.
Both verbs in Mark 1:15 are present imperatives, calling for a response that is not merely a passing religious moment.
But notice something important.
Jesus does not say, “Make yourself righteous, prove that your repentance is good enough, and afterward you may believe.”
Neither does He say, “Claim to believe in Me while remaining comfortably committed to the sins from which I call you.”
He commands repentance and faith together.
And this is where we must be careful.
The order in which two commands appear in a sentence does not, by itself, establish a universal chronological sequence for how salvation happens in every human heart.
Jesus is announcing that the kingdom of God has drawn near.
The proper response is to turn from sin and trust the good news.
Repentance and faith are distinguishable, but they are inseparably connected in a genuine response to Christ.
You cannot meaningfully turn toward Jesus as Savior while deliberately insisting that the sin He came to save you from must remain your master.
And you cannot practice Christian repentance apart from turning toward the God whose mercy makes salvation possible.
But there is another passage that makes this question even more profound.
Acts 11:18 records the response of Jewish believers after hearing how God had welcomed Gentiles into the fellowship of salvation.
They glorified God and declared:
“Then hath God also to the Gentiles granted repentance unto life.” — Acts 11:18, KJV
Read that again.
God granted repentance.
The Greek expression is:
τὴν μετάνοιαν εἰς ζωὴν ἔδωκεν
Tēn metanoian eis zōēn edōken.
“He gave repentance leading to life.”
The word ἔδωκεν (edōken) means “gave” or “granted.”
And μετάνοιαν (metanoian) refers to repentance.
This is not a minor detail.
The believers did not praise the Gentiles for somehow manufacturing enough moral determination to deserve entrance into God's family.
They glorified God because He had opened the way of life to people whom many had previously regarded as outsiders.
The wider context matters.
Peter had been explaining how the Holy Spirit came upon the Gentiles as they received the Gospel. God's saving welcome was not restricted by ethnic background or by humanly imposed barriers.
And the believers recognized the divine grace behind what had happened.
Repentance unto life was something God had granted.
That does not mean human beings never genuinely repent.
They do.
God's gracious work does not make the human response imaginary.
It means that repentance is never a reason for sinners to boast as though they had independently earned salvation.
Think about that.
The very turning toward God that exposes your need for mercy is itself something Scripture connects to His gracious initiative.
You may have spent years treating repentance like an admission fee you must pay before approaching Christ.
But repentance is not the purchase price of salvation.
Jesus Christ has already accomplished what no sinner could accomplish through His sinless life, sacrificial death, and resurrection.
We are not saved because our sorrow is deep enough.
We are not justified because our tears are numerous enough.
We are not forgiven because our promises are finally impressive enough.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 leaves no room for boasting in ourselves.
And yet grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace brings sinners to the Savior who calls them to repent.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because there is a kind of preaching that makes people afraid to approach Jesus until they have already repaired themselves.
And there is another kind of preaching that tells people they can receive Jesus without ever confronting the sin that is destroying them.
Neither should be confused with the full biblical message.
The Gospel is not “Clean yourself up, and then Christ will consider saving you.”
But neither is it “Keep worshiping your sin, and call that faith.”
The Gospel announces a crucified and risen Savior who receives sinners by grace and transforms those who belong to Him.
Now consider the third passage.
Paul writes to Timothy about correcting those who oppose the truth, instructing the Lord's servant to do so with gentleness:
“If God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth.” — 2 Timothy 2:25, KJV
The Greek includes the remarkable expression:
μήποτε δώῃ αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς μετάνοιαν
Mēpote dōē autois ho theos metanoian.
“Perhaps God may grant them repentance.”
Again, repentance is something God grants.
And notice the setting.
Paul is not describing a preacher humiliating sinners into submission.
He is instructing a servant of the Lord to correct opponents gently, patiently, and without quarrelsomeness.
Why?
Because the deepest change in the human heart cannot be forced through anger, intimidation, or religious performance.
Truth must be proclaimed.
Error must be corrected.
People are responsible for their response.
But God is the one upon whom the servant ultimately depends for the gift of repentance.
That should change the way we speak to struggling believers.
It should change the way parents pray for wandering children.
It should change the way churches respond to people trapped in destructive patterns.
And it should change the way you approach God when your own heart feels stubborn, cold, or spiritually exhausted.
You can pray:

“Lord, I know I need to repent. But even my heart feels resistant. Please open my eyes to the truth. Help me hate what is destroying me. Help me love what is pleasing to You. Turn my heart toward Christ.”
That is not an excuse for remaining in sin.
It is an acknowledgment that genuine spiritual transformation requires God's grace.
But now we must return to the original question.
Does repentance come before faith, or does faith in Christ produce repentance?
The biblical answer requires more care than a simple slogan.
Mark 1:15 commands both repentance and faith as the appropriate response to the Gospel.
Acts 11:18 and 2 Timothy 2:25 teach that repentance is granted by God.
Other passages illuminate their relationship.
Acts 20:21 speaks of “repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Acts 26:20 calls people to repent, turn to God, and demonstrate repentance through their deeds.
In Acts 16:31, Paul tells the Philippian jailer:
“Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved.”
John's Gospel repeatedly emphasizes believing in Jesus for eternal life.
And 1 Thessalonians 1:9 describes believers turning to God from idols to serve the living and true God.
Taken together, these passages do not establish a stopwatch-like sequence in which every person must first complete one spiritual action before beginning the other.
Christians across different theological traditions have explained the relationship somewhat differently.
Some emphasize repentance and faith as two inseparable aspects of conversion: turning away from sin and turning toward Christ.
Others emphasize that God first renews the sinner's heart, enabling both repentance and faith.
Still others emphasize God's preceding grace, which enables a genuine human response without eliminating the possibility of resisting that grace.
These are meaningful theological differences, and Scripture should not be made to say more than a particular passage actually says.
Yet the central Gospel truth remains clear.
No sinner earns salvation by repenting well enough, and no genuine saving faith treats Christ's call to repentance as irrelevant.
Repentance is not a competing Savior.
Faith is not a license to continue in rebellion.
And Jesus is not waiting at the finish line for you to achieve moral perfection before He will receive you.
He is the Savior to whom sinners are called to come.
There is a difference between a repentant person who still struggles with sin and an unrepentant person who has made peace with it.
One may fall and grieve because the sin contradicts the Lord they love.
The other may defend, celebrate, or excuse the sin while refusing Christ's authority.
But even here, we must be humble.
We cannot always measure another person's spiritual condition by looking at one isolated moment of failure.
Nor should we reassure ourselves merely because we occasionally feel guilty.
The question is not whether you have ever fallen after professing faith.
The question is whether you are turning toward Christ in trust and surrender, or deliberately turning away from Him.
Remember Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
Then, under pressure, he denied knowing Him.
Three times.
Imagine the weight of that failure.
The voice of his own denial.
The memory of his confidence.
The unbearable realization that he had done exactly what he insisted he would never do.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Peter remembered the Lord's words and wept bitterly.
But Peter's tears were not the price of his restoration.
The risen Jesus came to His disciples.
And in John 21, He dealt personally with Peter, calling him again to love and service.
Peter's story does not make denial harmless.
It makes the mercy of Christ magnificent.
The Savior Peter denied was the Savior who restored him.
Now think about the younger son in Luke 15.
He demanded his inheritance, left his father's house, and wasted what he had received.
Eventually, he found himself in humiliation and hunger.
Then Scripture says something extraordinary.
“And when he came to himself…” — Luke 15:17, KJV
He recognized what he had done.
He resolved to return.
He confessed his sin.
But before he could finish the speech he had prepared, his father received him with compassion.
The son did not return with an impressive record of reform.
He returned acknowledging his guilt and depending upon mercy.
And the father did not celebrate the rebellion.
He celebrated the return.
This parable is not a technical explanation of the precise logical order of regeneration, faith, and repentance.
It is a picture of the astonishing mercy of God toward the lost who return.
And perhaps that is the picture someone reading this desperately needs.
Because somewhere, someone is convinced they have gone too far.
A husband who has hidden an addiction from his family.
A woman carrying the shame of decisions she cannot undo.
A young believer who keeps falling into the same temptation.
A church leader who looks spiritually strong in public but knows how much darkness has been tolerated in private.
A person who grew up hearing about Jesus but has never truly surrendered to Him.
Perhaps someone has even begun to wonder whether God is tired of hearing their prayers.
Listen carefully.
The cross does not minimize your sin.
It reveals how serious sin truly is.
But the cross also reveals how far the love of God went to redeem sinners.
Jesus did not die because humanity needed a little encouragement.
He died because we needed a Savior.
And He rose again because death would not have the final word.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every relationship.
Not after we conquered every temptation.
Christ died for sinners.
But do not misunderstand this grace.
The Christ who receives sinners also calls them to follow Him.
He does not promise that discipleship will be effortless.
He does not pretend that obedience is optional.
And He does not teach us to rename darkness as light.
His grace forgives.
His truth confronts.
His Spirit sanctifies.
His love disciplines.
His mercy restores.
And His Gospel creates a new direction for those who belong to Him.
This is why repentance cannot be reduced to a single emotional experience.
There is an initial turning to God in conversion, and there is also an ongoing life of repentance as believers confess sin, reject it, and grow in holiness.
Even mature Christians continue to need the mercy of God.
First John 1:9 reminds believers of God's faithfulness and righteousness in forgiving and cleansing those who confess their sins.
And 2 Corinthians 7:10 distinguishes godly sorrow, which produces repentance, from worldly sorrow, which produces death.
Feeling terrible is not automatically the same thing as repenting.
Some people feel terrible because they were exposed.
Some feel terrible because they lost something.
Some feel terrible because their self-image has been shattered.
But godly sorrow directs us toward God.
It does not merely say, “I hate what happened to my reputation.”
It says, “Lord, I have sinned against You.”
And true repentance begins to bear fruit.
It may involve confession.
Restitution where appropriate.
Ending a destructive relationship.
Seeking accountability.
Making an apology without demanding immediate forgiveness.
Rejecting a habit that has been defended for years.
Accepting consequences rather than using religious language to escape responsibility.
But these actions are not payments that purchase justification.
They are fitting expressions of a heart turning toward God.
We are not saved by the fruit of repentance. But genuine repentance is not content to remain forever fruitless.
And what about the believer who is still struggling?
What about the person who has sincerely confessed sin, yet continues to fight powerful habits?
Do not confuse the presence of a battle with proof that God has abandoned you.
At the same time, do not confuse the existence of a battle with permission to stop resisting.
Bring your struggle into the light.
Seek wise pastoral help.
Find trustworthy Christian accountability.
Where addiction, trauma, or other serious difficulties are involved, appropriate professional care may also be an important part of seeking help.
And above all, keep looking to Christ.
Not because your struggle is insignificant.
But because your Savior is sufficient.
Philippians 1:6 expresses Paul's confidence that God would complete the good work He had begun among the Philippian believers.
Christian hope is not confidence in our own flawless determination.
It is confidence in the faithfulness of God.
And now I want to return to that man sitting outside the church.
The one who could not bring himself to open the door.
Imagine he finally walks inside.
He sits in the back, hoping nobody notices.
The preacher speaks about repentance.
For a moment, his heart sinks.
Here it comes, he thinks.
Another reminder of everything I have failed to become.
But then he hears the Gospel.
Not a message that excuses his sin.
Not a message that tells him to stop caring about holiness.
A message about Jesus Christ, crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
A message about grace that cannot be earned.
A message about repentance that God grants.
A message about faith that rests upon the Savior rather than the sinner's ability to save himself.
And suddenly, the question begins to change.
Instead of asking, “Have I made myself worthy enough to come to Christ?”
He begins asking, “Why have I been running from the only One who can save me?”
He realizes that he does not need to manufacture a perfect spiritual performance before coming to Jesus.
He needs Jesus.
He needs to turn from sin.
He needs to trust the Savior.
He needs the mercy he cannot earn and the transformation he cannot accomplish apart from God's grace.
And perhaps, for the first time in years, his prayer becomes painfully simple.

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Teach me to repent. Help me trust You. Change what I cannot change by my own strength. I surrender myself to You.”
Not a magic formula.
Not words that guarantee salvation merely because they are repeated.
But an honest expression of the repentance and faith to which the Gospel calls us.
And perhaps that is where you are right now.
Not outside a church.
But at the doorway of surrender.
You have spent so long debating whether you have repented enough that you have forgotten the One to whom repentance points.
You have examined your emotions.
Measured your tears.
Counted your failures.
Compared your spiritual progress with somebody else's.
And somewhere in that exhausting process, you have begun looking more at yourself than at Christ.
But your hope was never meant to rest on the perfection of your repentance.
Your hope rests in the perfection of your Redeemer.
Repentance does not make Jesus willing to save. Jesus is the Savior whose grace calls sinners to repentance and faith.
That is the difference between trying to purchase mercy and receiving mercy through Christ.
So does repentance come before faith?
In Mark 1:15, Jesus names repentance before believing, but the verse does not settle every theological question about their precise order.
Does faith in Christ produce repentance?

Faith and repentance are deeply interconnected, and genuine trust in Christ leads to a life of turning from sin. Yet Scripture also explicitly teaches that God grants repentance, so we should not portray it merely as a human achievement produced independently of divine grace.
The safest biblical conclusion is this:

God graciously calls sinners through the Gospel to repent and believe in Jesus Christ. Repentance and saving faith belong together, and the Christian life continues in trusting Christ and turning from sin.
You do not need to solve every theological debate before responding to the Gospel.
You need the Savior whom the Gospel proclaims.

And if you are already His, you need to keep returning to His Word, confessing your sins, trusting His promises, and walking in the grace that teaches us to deny ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people pretending they have never failed.
But to keep pointing broken, struggling, growing, and searching people toward the truth of Jesus Christ.
From hiding to confession.
From self-righteousness to dependence upon Christ.
From spiritual confusion to biblical understanding.
From the weight of sin to the mercy of the crucified and risen Savior.
And if this message has exposed something in your own heart, please do not let it become another article you read, feel, and forget.
You do not have to publish the details of your struggle. God already knows them.
And if you have experienced Christ's restoring mercy, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may encourage someone who thinks restoration is impossible.
Because a world overflowing with spiritual noise desperately needs the truth of God's Word.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow in your understanding of Christ, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not extracted through guilt or pressure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
These items are not the reason we preach Christ. They are simply another way to encourage faith, spark conversations, and express our appreciation to those helping the ministry continue.
Those free resources matter to us.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is losing hope.
Speak the truth of Christ with love.
Because the Gospel does not belong to those who can afford to fund its proclamation.
It is good news for sinners who desperately need a Savior.
And before you leave, remember the question that brought us here.
Does repentance come before faith, or does faith produce repentance?
Perhaps the most important thing you can do today is stop treating that question as a reason to delay coming to Christ.
Hear His command.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask God for the grace to turn from what is destroying you.
Trust in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again.
And walk with Him in the newness of life that His grace makes possible.
Because the greatest scandal is not that sinners have fallen so terribly.
It is that the sinless Son of God willingly bore the shame and judgment sinners deserved, so that those who trust in Him might be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
And the greatest grace is not that God pretends our sins never mattered.
It is that Jesus Christ paid the price we could never pay.
You may have spent years trying to become worthy enough to return to Jesus, when the whole time your only hope was the mercy of the Jesus you needed to return to.
